h1: The 6 Best 30-Laptop Charging Carts of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 charging carts built for 30 laptops, Chromebooks and tablets, scored on bay design, security, cable management and fleet fit.
summary: The Pearington 30-device cart is the one to buy: 30 locked bays plus two bonus outlets, with cable management built into the dividers. The POCHAR mixed-fleet model is the pick for schools juggling Chromebooks, iPads and laptops. The ALT Technology cart is a straightforward school workhorse, the ARTMAN adds a two-slot buffer, and the open POCHAR suits supervised classrooms that do not need a lock.
intro: The number on the box, 30, hides the question that decides whether a cart works in your building: thirty of what? A bay that fits a slim tablet may not take a 14 inch laptop in a thick protective case, and a cart with thirty slots but no room for charger bricks leaves cables dangling across the carpet. Fleet type and case thickness matter more than the headline count.

We ranked six carts built for thirty devices and scored them on the Primea framework, weighting bay design, device compatibility, security and cable management most heavily. Larger carts that merely exceed thirty, such as 36 or 42 port models, were left out, because they solve a different procurement problem. Every cart here lists thirty bays, and none lists exact prices, only price brackets.

products.name: Pearington 30 Device Mobile Charging/Storage Cart for iPads, Tablets, Laptop
products.verdict: 30 locked bays, two bonus outlets and tidy cable dividers. The cart that thinks about the cables.
products.description:
Pearington builds its cart around 30 bays for storing and locking devices, plus two bonus outlets that let you charge 32 items in total. Slots are sized for screens up to 13 inches, and cable management lives in the dividers, so each device's lead stays in its own channel instead of tangling with its neighbours.

It ranks first over the POCHAR carts because the details are stated and the bonus outlets cover a teacher laptop or hotspot. The tradeoff is the 13 inch screen limit: 14 inch Chromebooks in cases will not fit, and full assembly is required, so budget an afternoon. It sits in the $200 to $500 bracket.

Best for schools with tablets and 13 inch laptops that value organised cabling. Measure your cased devices before ordering.
products.idealFor: Schools with tablets and small laptops who want tidy cabling.
products.skipIf: Your Chromebooks are 14 inches or larger in cases.

products.name: POCHAR 30 Unit Device Charging Station for Chromebook, iPad, 14'' Laptop
products.verdict: Named for Chromebooks, iPads and 14 inch laptops, so one cart serves a mixed fleet.
products.description:
POCHAR's 30-unit station is positioned for mixed device fleets, with its title naming Chromebooks, iPads and 14 inch laptops together. Thirty-device capacity is stated, and the 14 inch figure is the key difference from the Pearington's 13 inch slots.

It ranks second since the listing carries fewer details than the Pearington's: no outlet count or cable-management description appears. What it does give is flexibility, because a district that bought three kinds of device can park them in one cart. Compared with the K-12 POCHAR below, it trades classroom branding for broader fleet coverage.

Choose it when your devices vary in size. Confirm bay depth for cased units before you commit, since the listing does not state it.
pros: Named for a mixed device fleet
products.idealFor: Schools running Chromebooks, iPads and laptops side by side.
products.skipIf: You need documented cable channels or extra outlets.

products.name: POCHAR 30 Devices 14'' Screen Laptop Charging Cart for K-12 Classrooms
products.verdict: A 30-device cart marketed squarely at K-12 classrooms with 14 inch laptops.
products.description:
This POCHAR variant is aimed at K-12 classrooms and states a 14 inch screen size with 30-device capacity. For a school whose Chromebooks all share one form factor, that stated size is more useful than a mixed-fleet promise.

It lands third because it sacrifices the tablet-friendly flexibility of the other POCHAR and shares its missing details: no outlet count and no description of how cables are managed. Against the Pearington it wins on screen size and loses on documentation. Both sit in the $200 to $500 bracket.

Buy it for a laptop-only classroom set where the device is the standard 14 inch Chromebook. If tablets are in the mix, step up one rank.
products.idealFor: Classroom sets of identical 14 inch Chromebooks.
products.skipIf: Your fleet includes tablets or varying sizes.

products.name: ALT Technology 30-Bay Mobile School Charging Cart Station for Chromebook, Tablet
products.verdict: A 30-bay mobile school cart for Chromebooks and tablets from a dedicated education supplier.
products.description:
ALT Technology's cart is described as a 30-bay mobile school charging station for Chromebooks and tablets. The title names both device types, which makes it a safe fit for K-12 deployments that standardise on a smaller form factor.

It ranks fourth because the listing offers the least detail of the main four: no screen size, no outlet count and no cabling notes. We rank the Pearington and POCHAR carts higher for documenting more. ALT is a reasonable way to cross-check a quote if your district already buys through an education vendor.

It suits Chromebook and tablet fleets under standard school conditions. Ask the seller for bay dimensions before ordering if you use rugged cases.
products.idealFor: Chromebook and tablet fleets bought through school suppliers.
products.skipIf: You need larger laptops or documented cabling.

products.name: ARTMAN Mobile Charging Cart Station, 30+2 Bay Storage Cabinet for Chromebook, Tablet
products.verdict: A 30+2 bay cabinet with a small buffer above 30, but with no review history yet.
products.description:
ARTMAN lists a 30+2 bay storage cabinet for Chromebooks and tablets, which gives you two spare slots above the headline count. That buffer is handy for loaner devices, a teacher unit or a device awaiting repair.

It ranks fifth because it sits in the $500 and up bracket, the priciest of the six, and because it is a new listing with no meaningful ownership history. Against the Pearington, which also delivers a 32-device total for less, the ARTMAN offers a cabinet form factor and little else on paper.

It works for buyers who want a fully enclosed cabinet and can afford the premium. Treat it with caution until owner feedback builds up.
products.idealFor: Buyers wanting a small spare-slot buffer in an enclosed cabinet.
products.skipIf: You want a proven track record or a lower price.

products.name: POCHAR 30 Devices Open Laptop Charging Cart for iPads, Tablets
products.verdict: An open-design 30-device cart for supervised classrooms. No lock, so no overnight security.
products.description:
This POCHAR uses an open design with room for 30 devices, aimed at iPads and tablets. Without doors it lets students grab and return devices quickly, and teachers can see at a glance whether anything is missing.

The lack of a lock is why it ranks last: it gives no theft protection after hours unless the room itself is secure. The closed POCHAR and Pearington carts offer locked storage and are better for shared hallways. Where the room is locked and supervised, open access is faster and avoids key management.

Best for a single classroom with a supervised routine. Skip it for carts that move between rooms or sit in corridors.
pros: Visible device check at a glance
products.idealFor: Supervised classrooms that value quick distribution.
products.skipIf: The cart sits in a corridor or moves between rooms.

methodology.description: We compared stated screen sizes and device types, because a 30-bay count means little if your cased devices do not fit.

methodology.title: Cable management
methodology.description: Carts that document divider channels or bonus outlets scored higher than those that leave cabling unstated.

methodology.title: Fleet flexibility
methodology.description: Mixed-fleet support and spare capacity were credited, since school device mixes change over time.

methodology.title: Listing transparency and price
methodology.description: Carts that state more details were ranked ahead of those with sparse listings or no ownership history, within each price bracket.

whatMatters.detail: Screen size is the number on the box, but the bay has to fit the device plus its protective case and charger. A 13 inch slot will refuse a 14 inch laptop. Measure a cased device, add an inch for the plug, and compare it with the bay dimensions in the listing.

A locked cart keeps devices safe overnight and between classes, while an open cart speeds distribution. Choose by where the cart lives. A cart in a corridor or shared lab needs a lock, and a cart inside one supervised classroom can go without. Check whether the listing says locking doors or open storage.

Thirty chargers in one cabinet can become a knot. Dividers with cable channels keep each lead separate and speed up daily collection. Look for the words cable management or channels in the description, and check whether chargers plug into a surge-protected strip inside the cart or need separate outlets.

Charging thirty devices draws real power, and a cart that stages or distributes the load protects the building circuit. Bonus outlets, like the Pearington's two, let you add a teacher laptop. Ask the seller how the cart is wired, and confirm the plug fits your classroom outlet.

Carts arrive flat-packed and weigh a lot when loaded. Assembly can take a couple of hours, and caster quality decides whether the cart rolls over thresholds. Check for stated assembly requirements, locking casters and a handle position that lets one person steer the loaded cart safely.

faq.q: Will a 30-device cart fit my 14 inch Chromebooks?
faq.a: Only if the bay says so. The Pearington lists slots up to 13 inches, while both POCHAR carts state 14 inch compatibility. Measure a cased Chromebook and compare it with the listing before ordering.

faq.q: What mistake do schools make buying charging carts?
faq.a: Buying for the bare device. Cases add width and depth, and chargers add bulk. A cart that fits a naked tablet can refuse the same tablet in a rugged case, so check dimensions with the case on.

faq.q: Is the ARTMAN worth the extra money over the Pearington?
faq.a: Rarely. The ARTMAN adds two bays in the $500 and up bracket but has no ownership history. The Pearington charges 32 devices in the $200 to $500 bracket, so it delivers similar capacity for less.

faq.q: Do these carts need much setup?
faq.a: Plan on assembly. The Pearington states that full assembly is required, and the others ship flat-packed too. Allow a couple of hours, two people for the lifting, and a flat floor so the casters roll straight.

faq.q: How should I care for a charging cart?
faq.a: Keep vents clear, route cables through the dividers and avoid daisy-chaining extension cords. On the Pearington, use the dividers so chargers do not pull on ports. Check the lock and casters each term.

faq.q: Can I use an open cart like the POCHAR for overnight storage?
faq.a: Only inside a locked room. The open POCHAR has no door lock, so it offers no protection on its own. For corridors or shared labs choose a locked cart such as the Pearington.

finalTake: For most schools the Pearington 30 Device cart is the one to buy: locked bays, two bonus outlets and cable management you can actually see in the listing. Pick the POCHAR mixed-fleet cart if your devices come in several sizes, the ALT Technology cart for a plain school workhorse, and the open POCHAR only for a supervised, lockable classroom. Treat the ARTMAN with caution until it has owner feedback.
